# Authority Instead of Substance: How AI Exposed the Emptiness of Expert Discourse

![oleg kholin](https://miro.medium.com/v2/da:true/resize:fill:64:64/0*4ekR81Udpiz2aMz6)

oleg kholin

3 hours ago

How AI Uncovered the Emptiness of a Significant Part of Contemporary Expert Literature

There is one peculiarity of contemporary expert, analytical and journalistic literature that becomes especially noticeable when one reads large volumes of texts: a remarkably high concentration of words combined with an extremely low density of content. Articles may run for several pages and look thorough, containing warnings, caveats, forecasts and recommendations, yet after reading them it often turns out that there is practically nothing to be extracted from them.

A characteristic example is the reasoning about the threats associated with the development of artificial intelligence and the potential breaking of modern public-key cryptography. Instead of a concrete analysis of the consequences, an assessment of timelines, vulnerable infrastructures and possible scenarios, the reader receives something like the following:

“Most likely, it won’t go smoothly. There will be many changes, and some of them — perhaps very many — will cause pain. Some of the things we rely on may break, and we will have to build them anew, and perhaps more than once.

But right now I feel more optimistic than I have in many years. The risks haven’t gone anywhere. But along with them have come opportunities that I could not have seen even a few years ago.

Take the threats seriously. Let them wake you up. And then get to work.

The only real way through this is to believe that we can get through, and to act.”

Formally, everything needed for a convincing expert statement is present here: an acknowledgment of risks, a balanced assessment of prospects, emotional support and a call to action. The text sounds confident, is carefully calibrated in its intonation and even inclines one toward a certain optimism. But if one tries to extract information from it, a curious situation emerges: there is practically no concrete content. What exactly will break; which infrastructures will come under threat; what the new opportunities consist in; what should be done and within what timeframe — the text does not answer these questions.

Perhaps the most precise literary illustration of this phenomenon can be found long before the appearance of large language models, in Isaac Asimov’s science-fiction novel Foundation. One of the episodes concerns a scholar who runs the solemn speech of a consul of the Galactic Empire through a decoder. The result turns out to be unexpected: once the rhetorical shell has been removed, practically nothing is left of the speech. Behind the pompous formulations, meant to demonstrate the grandeur and significance of imperial power, no corresponding informational content is to be found.

Today this literary device can be applied to a significant part of expert literature, and one does not necessarily even need a special decoder. It is enough to put a few simple questions to the text: what exactly is being claimed, on what grounds, which facts are cited, and what conclusions follow from the facts cited. Quite often, after such a procedure, far less remains than one could have expected from the original volume of the publication.

It is particularly interesting that an analogous experiment can be carried out with contemporary language models. Try asking the leading systems among the top ten most popular AI models to discuss the problem of empty expert language. One can expect that their answers will to a large extent reproduce the very same stylistic construction that is to be analyzed. There will appear arguments about the need for a cautious approach, about separating several independent aspects, about rethinking terminology and seeking more precise definitions.

“I would be more cautious about this hypothesis.”

“Here I would split your thought into two independent parts.”

“Let’s try to call this something different.”

In themselves, such phrases are not mistaken. Sometimes caution really is necessary, a complex thought is useful to break down into its components, and terminology does have to be clarified. The problem arises when such constructions cease to serve analysis and begin to replace it. Instead of testing an argument, a cautious attitude toward it is proposed; instead of identifying causes, a division into aspects; instead of a substantive answer, a renaming of the problem. What arises is an imitation of intellectual work, in which the outward form of reasoning is preserved even in the absence of any noticeable progress of thought.

Why does this happen? One possible explanation has to do with the materials on which language models are trained. The modern internet contains colossal volumes of texts created by experts, analysts, consultants, politicians and the authors of numerous industry publications. A significant part of this body consists of texts in which a recognizable style, the right intonation and a persuasive composition matter almost more than informational novelty.

To this is added the influence of model-tuning procedures. Testers and raters prefer certain forms of response: polite, balanced, cautious, structured. The model gradually absorbs not only linguistic regularities but also a notion of what an acceptable response should look like. If a cautious caveat is received better than direct disagreement, and an enumeration of aspects looks preferable to a check of the initial premise, the corresponding constructions gain an additional advantage.

As a result, a peculiar feedback loop arises. AI is trained on human texts, reproduces the speech constructions characteristic of them, and then receives additional reinforcement for using them. It turns out that artificial intelligence did not create the culture of verbose vacuity but inherited it, and learned to reproduce it with industrial efficiency.

Here, however, a more interesting question arises. Why did we begin to call such texts AI slop only after they came to be produced by an artificial intelligence device?

After all, the constructions themselves existed long before the appearance of generative models. The same universal warnings, ritual caveats, optimistic conclusions and calls to action were present for years in the publications of entirely real authors. They were read, quoted, published in professional journals, used in presentations and expert speeches. And by no means always was any greater substantive content demanded of them.

Perhaps the presence of a human author created a certain effect of trust. Behind the text stood a surname, a position, an organization, a professional reputation. The reader was inclined to assume that behind the right words lay corresponding competence, even if it was scarcely manifested in the text itself. The authority of the source partly compensated for the lack of content.

With artificial intelligence the situation has changed. When a similar text is generated by a machine, the reader begins to treat its content more attentively. It becomes noticeable that behind the smoothness of the formulations there may stand neither independent analysis, nor an original thought, nor even a clear understanding of the subject. What was previously perceived as the customary style of expert communication now receives a new name — AI slop.

But there is a certain unfairness in this name toward artificial intelligence itself. The machine did not invent the source material. It reproduced a linguistic environment that already existed, one in which substantive emptiness had long ago learned to look like professional competence. And if today we discover this emptiness in the answers of AI, perhaps we should ask ourselves why earlier it so rarely provoked a similar reaction.

It is precisely here that Asimov’s literary metaphor acquires an additional meaning. The consul’s decoder did not create the emptiness of the imperial speech — it merely made it possible to see what had been hidden behind its solemn form. Contemporary language models perform a partly similar function, albeit unintentionally. They reproduce the accumulated human discourse on such a scale that its stylistic features become more noticeable, and its substantive poverty ceases to be masked by the individuality of the author.

Perhaps artificial intelligence has turned out to be not so much the source of the problem as its largest-scale demonstrator. And then the question concerns not only the quality of the generated texts. It concerns the criteria by which we have grown accustomed to distinguishing expert knowledge from its verbal imitation.

Perhaps a curious inverse symmetry is revealed here. In contemporary art, a theoretical description is capable of endowing with value an artifact that in itself suggests to the viewer neither meaning nor artistic significance. In expert literature the opposite occurs: the author’s name, position, regalia and institutional affiliation endow with value a text that in itself may contain nothing but stylistically impeccable emptiness. In the first case interpretation elevates the artifact, in the second authority elevates the text. AI has inadvertently disrupted this construction: by separating the text from the social status of its producer, it has made visible the difference between the content of a statement and the value ascribed to it by the authority of its author. Perhaps this is precisely why what for decades was considered perfectly acceptable expert discourse suddenly came to be called AI slop when reproduced by a language model.

Instead of a postscript. One more paradox connected with this problem. The situation in which language models mistook the independently written works of literate students for texts created by AI has already been discussed earlier. The explanation seemed entirely logical: the models had been trained on large bodies of well-written, stylistically correct texts, and therefore academically correct human writing could be perceived by them as a characteristic product of machine generation.

However, this situation can now be considered from another side. If the model itself reproduces a verbose, stylistically impeccable but substantively unproductive discourse, then in evaluating a student’s work it may encounter the same features that are present in its own answers. It recognizes a familiar structure, a familiar composition, a familiar way of filling a text with correct but not necessarily informative formulations. The question arises: do we not sometimes take for signs of machine origin what are in fact signs of a long-established human culture of writing?

And here the problem goes beyond the reliability of AI detectors. The machine turns out to be at once a product of this culture, its reproducer and an instrument for evaluating the texts created within it. It can reproduce emptiness and then discover it in human work, without having any reliable way of establishing who exactly produced it.
